power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Executive functions (EF) are associated with weight management, yet the two common ways of measuring them, cognitive tasks and self-report questionnaires of everyday functioning, rarely agree.
The present study examined whether combining both types of measures reveals distinct profiles of EF and how these relate to age, body mass index (BMI), and eating behaviors.

Methods: Adults enrolled in a behavioral weight-loss intervention (N = 277; 84% women; mean BMI 33.9 kg/m²) completed diverse cognitive tasks tapping EF, the BRIEF-A, and the Dutch Eating Behavior Questionnaire.

Bayesian factor analyses captured task-based (inhibitory control, working memory) and self-reported (behavioral regulation, emotional regulation, metacognition) EF latent factors, which were entered into a latent profile analysis with age, BMI, and restrained, emotional, and external eating.
Results: Task-based and self-reported EF factors were essentially uncorrelated.

Three profiles emerged (entropy = 0.82): (i) higher EF task performance with few self-reported difficulties, (ii) lower EF task performance with few self-reported difficulties in older participants, and (iii) average EF task performance with more self-reported difficulties and the highest emotional and external eating.
BMI and restrained eating were similar across profiles.
Conclusions: Adults with similar BMI had distinct combinations of cognitive performance, everyday executive difficulties, and eating behaviors.
Emotional and external eating were linked to self-reported EF difficulties rather than EF task performance, suggesting that self-report EF measures add clinically relevant information.
Future work should test whether these profiles predict adherence and weight loss.

Despite growing interest in the role of EF in weight management, we identify three gaps that limit the current understanding.

First, the studies to date have primarily relied on performancebased cognitive tasks or self-report measures in isolation, yet it is unclear whether these measures capture distinct and/or complementary dimensions of health-related behavioral and cognitive control.
Second, prior research has often adopted variable-centered approaches, examining associations between individual EF components and obesity-related outcomes.
While informative, these approaches assume population homogeneity and may obscure meaningful inter-individual differences (Howard & Hoffman, 2018; Muthén & Muthén, 2000).

text.text: By integrating both performance-based and self-reported measures of executive functioning within a single analytical framework, LPA can provide a more comprehensive characterization of EF and reveal profiles that may not be detectable using traditional approaches.
If performance-based and selfreport measures capture distinct, but complementary aspects of EF, their combined use may enhance the precision of cognitive assessment in obesity research.
Thus, identifying subgroups of individuals with distinct EF profiles may inform the development of personalized intervention strategies that target specific cognitive and behavioral needs.
This study seeks to examine heterogeneity in EF among adults enrolled in a behavioral weight-loss intervention.

By integrating performance-based measures of inhibitory control and WM with self-reported measures of behavioral regulation, emotional regulation, and metacognition, we use a person-centered approach to identify patterns that may not be apparent when these dimensions are considered separately.
Specifically, the present study addresses three research questions: (RQ1) Are there distinct profiles when performance-based and self-reported dimensions of EF are jointly considered?
(RQ2) Are the identified EF profiles characterized by individual differences in age and Body Mass Index (BMI)?
(RQ3) Do individuals across these profiles differ in restrained, emotional, and external eating behaviors?
Healthy adults (i.e., 18 years old and above) were recruited through Cedars-Sinai's network of hospitals and clinics, in addition to community outreach strategies.
Flyers and digital advertisements targeting adults seeking weight loss were distributed across clinical, community, and educational settings across the United States.
Interested individuals accessed an eligibility screening questionnaire via a QR code.
Upon providing informed consent, eligible participants completed baseline assessments, including demographic characteristics, anthropometric measures, and cognitive tasks measuring EF.

Participants were considered ineligible if they met any of the following conditions: (i) concurrent enrollment in a weight-loss program or scheduled bariatric surgery, (ii) pregnancy, (iii) severe cognitive deficits or substantial visual or hearing impairments, or (iv) medical contraindications to weight loss (e.g., unstable coronary artery disease, end-stage disease, active cancer treatment, uncontrolled insulin-dependent diabetes, portal hypertension, or substance abuse).
The analyzed sample included 277 adults (233 female, mean age 43.51, SD = 11.73).

The demographic survey collected information on participants' date of birth, sex, race and ethnicity, and socioeconomic indicators, including education level, household income, marital status, and employment status.
It also assessed household composition (e.g., multigenerational living arrangements, single or partnered status, presence of children) and medical history.
All participants were provided with Bluetooth-enabled scales (WW Bluetooth Body Analysis Scale, Conair LLC, Stamford, CT).
Prior to measurement, participants were instructed to remove their shoes and any heavy outerwear.
For each measurement, participants stepped onto the center of the scale and stood upright with weight distributed evenly.
This procedure was performed in duplicates, and the average of the two measurements was also recorded.
Body mass index (BMI; kg/m²) was derived from these measures.

The present study aimed to identify latent profiles among adults enrolled in a behavioral weight-loss intervention to characterize heterogeneity in executive functioning, eating behaviors, age, and BMI.
Three main findings emerged.
First, when performance-based and self-reported measures of EF were considered jointly, three distinct and relatively balanced profiles were identified.
Importantly, these profiles did not simply order participants in a continuum from lower to higher scores on measures of EF, but reflected different configurations of EF profiles.
Second, the profiles differed by age, but showed little differentiation by BMI.
Third, emotional and external eating differed across profiles, whereas mean levels of restrained eating were similar across profiles.

Together, these findings highlight substantial heterogeneity in the cognitive and behavioral characteristics of individuals with elevated BMI, and provide further evidence that performance-based and self-reported measures of EF offer complementary information.

text.text: The present findings extend these conclusions to adults seeking to lose weight.
The LPA showed how these two types of measures combine to characterize different EF profiles, despite their apparent dissociation.
Profile 1 was characterized by relatively higher inhibitory control and WM with fewer reported difficulties in behavioral regulation, emotional regulation, and metacognition.
In contrast, Profile 2 showed relatively low performance-based EF despite reporting comparatively few everyday executive difficulties.
Profile 3 showed the opposite pattern: performance-based EF was approximately average, whereas they reported greater difficulties across the three BRIEF-A dimensions.
Thus, the profiles were differentiated not simply by overall EF level, but by the extent to which cognitive performance and perceived everyday executive functioning converged or diverged.

This reinforces the view that the capacity to perform efficiently on laboratory controlled tasks is not equivalent to successfully deploying executive control across complex everyday situations (Snyder et al., 2021), which are shaped by contextual demands, motivation, emotion, habits, environmental supports, and strategies that are largely absent when measuring EF with standardized cognitive tasks (Toplak et al., 2013; Roth et al., 2013).

This distinction is consistent with evidence from community-dwelling older adults showing only modest correspondence between selfreported everyday EF and performance on conventional cognitive measures (Meltzer et al., 2017).

text.text: Thus, lower performance-based EF among older individuals should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence of broader problems with everyday self-regulation.
In contrast, BMI contributed little to profile differentiation and remained close to the sample mean in all three profiles.
This finding should first be interpreted in light of the characteristics of the sample.

Participants were recruited for a behavioral weight-loss intervention, BMI showed less variation than would be expected in a population-based sample, which likely limited its contribution to profile differentiation.
Nevertheless, the absence of BMI differences is informative, as individuals with broadly similar levels of BMI showed different patterns of executive functioning and eating behavior.

This heterogeneity is consistent with prior LPA research among adults with overweight or obesity which identified subgroups differing in restrained eating, eating disinhibition, intuitive eating, or eating motivation despite similarly elevated BMI (Boulanger et al., 2024; Maltais-Lévesque et al., 2025).

text.text: The third research question examined whether the identified profiles differed in restrained, emotional, and external eating.
The clearest differences involved emotional and external eating.
Profile 3 was characterized by greater difficulties in behavioral regulation, emotional regulation, and metacognition, and also showed the highest scores on emotional and external eating.
Conversely, Profiles 1 and 2 both showed relatively lower emotional and external eating despite differing considerably in performance-based EF.
Profile 2 is again especially informative: poorer task-based EF was not accompanied by elevated emotional or external eating.
Taken together, this pattern suggests that these eating tendencies aligned more closely with perceived difficulties in everyday executive regulation than with performance-based EF capacity.
This finding is consistent with previous research on everyday self-regulatory difficulties and eating behavior.

text.text: Heterogeneity in EF, therefore, may be particularly relevant to reactive or cue-driven eating tendencies rather than to dietary restraint per se.
These findings have methodological and clinical implications.
From an assessment perspective, relying exclusively on either cognitive tasks or self-report measures may provide an incomplete characterization of EF.

Individuals who perform poorly under standardized cognitive demands do not necessarily experience substantial executive difficulties in everyday life, while individuals with average cognitive performance may nevertheless report meaningful problems with behavioral, emotional, and metacognitive regulation.
Thus, a multivariate approach to assessment may be particularly valuable when the goal is to understand self-regulation in complex health behaviors.
The profiles may also provide a useful framework for studying heterogeneity in response to weight-loss interventions.
Individuals with similar BMI may enter treatment with very different combinations of cognitive capacity, everyday executive functioning difficulties, and eating tendencies.

Whether these baseline profiles predict adherence, engagement, or weight-loss success remains to be tested prospectively, and establishing such associations is a necessary step before drawing conclusions about profile-specific or personalized intervention strategies.
This study has several limitations.
First, the analyses were cross-sectional and based on baseline data, precluding conclusions about temporal or causal relationships among EF, eating behavior, and BMI.

Second, both the BRIEF-A and DEBQ are self-report measures and therefore, their closer correspondence may partly reflect shared method variance rather than a uniquely Executive functioning and eating behavior profiles among weight management participants This manuscript is a preprint stronger relationship between everyday EF and eating behavior.
Third, the sample consisted predominantly of women, was relatively highly educated, and included adults actively seeking weight loss, which may limit generalizability to other populations.
The restricted BMI distribution may also have reduced the ability of BMI to differentiate profiles, and BMI itself is a relatively coarse indicator of adiposity and metabolic health.

Fourth, although several tasks were used to measure EF, the task battery did not provide sufficient measures to capture a richer multidimensional structure encompassing theoretically separable components such as inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and WM (Karr et al., 2018; Miyake et al., 2000; Yangüez et al., 2024).

text.text: Finally, LPA solutions are sample-dependent.

Although the retained three-profile model showed good classification and reasonably balanced profile sizes, replication in an independent sample is necessary to establish the stability and generalizability of the profiles.
The present study identified three distinct profiles among adults seeking weight loss characterized by different EF phenotypes, age, and eating behaviors.
Individuals with similar BMI showed different cognitive and behavioral characteristics.
Poorer performance-based EF was not necessarily associated with greater everyday executive difficulties or elevated emotional and external eating.
Instead, emotional and external eating were most pronounced among individuals reporting greater difficulties with behavioral, emotional, and metacognitive regulation in everyday life.

These findings underscore the complementary information provided by performance-based and self-report measures of EF on understanding the relationship between cognition, overweight or obesity, and eating behaviors.

Future longitudinal analyses should determine whether these cognitive-behavioral profiles predict adherence and response to behavioral weight-loss interventions and, ultimately, whether they can inform more precisely targeted intervention strategies.

For the performance-based EF tasks, competing measurement models were tested to examine the latent structure of EF.

Specifically, we compared (1) one-factor model representing a common EF construct; (2a) two-factor model A with Inhibitory Control and WM, where n-back loads onto WM; (2b) two-factor model B which has n-back task loading onto both constructs Inhibitory Control and WM; (3a) bifactor model consisting of the two first-order factors of model (2a) loading onto a higher-order factor; (3b) bifactor model consisting of the two first-order factors of model (2b) loading onto a higher-order factor.

Note that hierarchical and bifactor models differ in whether the general factor influences the observed measures indirectly through the first-order factors (hierarchical) or directly alongside orthogonal specific factors (bifactor).

Model fit was evaluated using the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), Deviance Information Criterion (DIC), and Widely Applicable Information Criterion (WAIC) and Leave-One-Out cross-validation Information Criterion (LOOIC).
Lower values indicate better fit.
The best-fitting measurement model for each assessment modality was retained, and individual factor scores were extracted for use in the subsequent latent profile analyses.
